sourdough-baking.how: Hands-on sourdough and focaccia workshops run by cafes and kitchens; a starter kit is often sent home.

artisan-bread-baking.how: SkillsFuture-funded multi-day baking courses are offered by private training providers.
artisan-bread-baking.venue: Coursemology (Bake Artisan and Decorative Breads course)

cheese-making.how: No regular public cheesemaking class found; Alliance Francaise has hosted one-off masterclasses (a visiting cheesemaker, small fresh cheese made to take home) and cheese tastings.

homebrewing-beer.how: Short workshops teach brewing and bottling a small batch to take home; a local homebrew community and the iBrew Challenge also exist.
homebrewing-beer.venue: Lion Brewery Co (Brew Your Own Beer workshop)

sake-making.how: A local sake-brewing outfit runs a 2.5 hour workshop where you make your own sake mash and taste three sakes.
sake-making.venue: Fermentopia (sake-making workshop; venue name taken from listing URL, not confirmed)

sake-tasting.how: Sommelier-led sake tastings and appreciation sessions; NYP also lists an Introduction to Sake short course (no intake open when checked).
sake-tasting.venue: Sake appreciation sessions via SeekSophie; NYP Introduction to Sake course

whisky-tasting.how: Whisky bars and independent bottlers run guided tasting sets and appreciation workshops.

whisky-society.how: The Scotch Malt Whisky Society relaunched a small Singapore branch in late 2023 that works with partner bars and runs pairing dinners.

latte-art.how: Many cafes and roasters run latte art and barista classes in small groups.
latte-art.venue: Nineteen95 The Espresso Bar (latte art class)

coffee-roasting.how: A local roastery runs workshops (including large groups) and roasting-focused programmes; venue details not verified.

tea-ceremony.how: Urasenke and Omotesenke associations give live tea ceremony demonstrations at Gardens by the Bay during the seasonal sakura display; regular hands-on lessons not verified.
tea-ceremony.venue: Gardens by the Bay, Flower Dome

sushi-making.how: Leisure nigiri or roll classes at a sushi school, plus a longer professional sushi programme at At-Sunrice.

dim-sum-making.how: SkillsFuture-approved two-day courses covering bao, dumplings and egg tarts, plus shorter private classes.

pasta-and-general-cooking-classes.how: Cooking-class marketplaces list chef-led hands-on classes such as pasta making across Singapore.

chocolate-making.how: Two-hour workshops roast, winnow, grind, temper and mould cacao into a bar; some venues keep a cacao plant.

beekeeping-honey.how: Rooftop and community apiaries run beekeeping workshops with honey tasting (SUSS BEE AMAZED Garden; Nutrinest at Sembawang).

mixology.how: Accredited ITE Certificate of Competency in Art of Mixology (14 hours) and a one-day SkillsFuture@PA bartending workshop.
mixology.venue: ITE College West (CoC in Art of Mixology)

wine-tasting-wset.how: WSET Levels 1-3 with tastings are run by Fine Wines SG; SkillsFuture credit usable.

fermentation-kombucha.how: Beginner kombucha, kefir and kimchi workshops; one 2-hour session sends you home with a SCOBY starter kit.

butchery.how: No butchery or sausage-making class found; there are butcher shops and an Asian cooking class at Huber's Butchery.

hawker-crawling.how: Hundreds of hawker centres; Maxwell Food Centre in Tanjong Pagar has about 100 stalls.

stamp-collecting.how: SingPost Philatelic Bureau serves collectors; CS Philatelic Agency is a private dealer; the Association of Singapore Philatelists organises events (Philatelic Museum status uncertain).

coin-collecting.how: Singapore International Coin Fair is a large annual event; the Singapore Mint and numismatic dealers also serve collectors.

trading-cards.how: Card Arena (Suntec City) hosts weekly tournaments; Card Nation and Cardboard Collectible run Magic, Pokemon and other events.

vinyl-records.how: Dozens of record shops, e.g. Red Point Record Warehouse with listening stations.

watch-collecting.how: Collector meetups such as the Watch-o-holics Anonymous Meetup group and the members-only 33Club at Raffles Place.

sneaker-collecting.how: Specialist stores like Limited Edt (Queensway) and the annual Sneaker Con SEA convention with a trading pit.

toy-collecting.how: Singapore Toy, Game and Comic Convention (STGCC) historically drew tens of thousands with exclusive figures; recent editions not confirmed.
toy-collecting.venue: STGCC (Singapore Toy, Game and Comic Convention)

comic-collecting.how: Singapore Comic Con is an annual event with exhibitors and collectibles; dedicated comic shops not verified here.

birdwatching.how: NSS Bird Group runs regular walks and surveys; Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve has hides and migratory shorebirds. Walk registration needs an NSS account from March 2026.
birdwatching.venue: Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve / Nature Society Singapore Bird Group

butterfly-watching.how: Nature Society's Butterfly Interest Group runs walks and events.
butterfly-watching.venue: Nature Society Singapore Butterfly Interest Group

rock-fossil-collecting.how: No fossil or rock fieldwork in Singapore; you can view specimens at the Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum or buy from shops (unverified).
rock-fossil-collecting.venue: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum

whale-watching.how: No regular whale-watching tours; cetaceans are rarely seen in Singapore waters (the museum's sperm whale was a stranded carcass).

train-spotting.how: Only MRT/LRT plus the short KTM shuttle to Woodlands; Tanjong Pagar station closed to trains in 2011 and no mainline or steam operations.

geocaching.how: Hundreds to 1,000+ caches island-wide, from parks to malls, via the Geocaching app.

japanese-language.how: Private language schools with native Japanese teachers run beginner courses; universities and community clubs also teach it.

tamil-language.how: NUS Centre for Language Studies runs a Level 1 Tamil course with no prerequisites (online/Saturday sessions, subsidies for citizens).

spanish-language.how: University language centres and private schools offer Spanish courses; no specific current class was verified.

french-language.how: Alliance Francaise de Singapour is the French cultural centre and runs French courses for adults.

german-language.how: The Goethe-Institut Singapore teaches German at all levels.

korean-language.how: The Korean Cultural Centre in Singapore offers Korean language classes.

sign-language.how: SADeaf runs a four-level Singapore Sign Language programme (weekday evenings, also online) open to adults.

language-exchange.how: Informal language-exchange meetups exist on Meetup-style platforms; I did not verify a specific active group.

toastmasters.how: Many English Toastmasters clubs meet in community clubs; the Bukit Timah CC club is listed on OnePA as free.

debate.how: No dedicated adult public debating club verified; impromptu-speaking Table Topics at Toastmasters is the closest, plus school/university debate circuits.

book-club.how: NLB's LearnX programme runs volunteer-led reading communities; the Singapore Literature Book Club meets monthly at Central Library; Silent Book Club also meets monthly.
book-club.venue: Singapore Literature Book Club (NLB, Central Library)

museums.how: The National Museum of Singapore and many other museums are open daily.

art-gallery.how: National Gallery Singapore holds large Southeast Asian art collections.

wartime-history.how: The Changi Museum covers the Japanese occupation and POW history.

heritage-trails.how: NHB publishes self-guided trails (e.g. Kampong Gelam, Little India) via Roots.gov.sg.

history-walks.how: Time Out lists multiple guided historical trails and tours in Singapore.

public-lectures.how: NLB and museums host free or cheap public talks.

creative-writing.how: Sing Lit Station runs writing programmes and workshops.

poetry-slam.how: Spoken-word open-mic nights run regularly, e.g. Layl Ash-Shayr at Wardah Books; the Speak slam series started in 2013 (current status unknown).

genealogy.how: NLB and Archives hold records and a family-history guide; Genealogy Society Singapore and FamilySearch occasionally run seminars, but no regular classes found.
genealogy.venue: National Library Board family history resources

ancient-ruins-excavation.how: Singapore has no ancient monuments; the oldest dug layers (Fort Canning) are around 14th century, so field schools mean travel abroad.

philosophy-cafe.how: Practical Philosophy Meetup holds weekly discussions, and the Philosophy Cafe has run monthly at Gone Fishing Cafe (current status unclear).

moocs.how: Online courses are accessible from anywhere; SkillsFuture subsidises many, though this is not a Singapore-specific venue.

chinese-calligraphy.how: Short workshops and a 12-lesson course teach brush calligraphy with ink and brushes provided.
chinese-calligraphy.venue: NTU Chinese Calligraphy Workshop / Visual Arts Centre

cultural-heritage-centres.how: The Indian Heritage Centre in Little India documents South Asian heritage.

archival-research.how: The National Archives of Singapore lets the public search records.

science-museum.how: Science Centre Singapore is a large interactive science museum.

yoga.how: Many studios and community-club classes exist; no single specific class was verified.

pilates.how: Pilates studios are widely available; not verified individually.

meditation.how: Kong Meng San Phor Kark See Monastery's meditation hall runs meditation courses.
meditation.venue: Kong Meng San Phor Kark See Monastery

tai-chi.how: Free tai chi/taiji groups meet in community clubs and parks, e.g. Linkhall Woodlands.

qigong.how: A free Shaolin Neijing Yizhichan Qigong class meets Wednesday mornings at Chai Chee.
qigong.venue: Ping An RN interest group (Chai Chee Rd hard court)

volunteering.how: SG Cares and NVPC list many volunteering openings.

community-gardening.how: NParks' Community in Bloom supports over 2,000 resident gardening groups and community gardens.

temple-activities.how: Temples, mosques, churches and Hindu temples welcome visitors; Sri Mariamman Temple is the oldest Hindu temple.

mentoring.how: Social service agencies and schools recruit volunteer mentors; no specific programme was verified.

support-groups.how: Peer-support volunteering exists via NCSS and Silver Ribbon, and Samaritans of Singapore runs a 24h hotline; open public support meetings were not found.

onsen.how: Japanese-style onsen exist, e.g. Yunomori Onsen & Spa and Ikeda Spa.

sauna.how: The Plunge Club offers a Finnish sauna.

massage.how: Spas and reflexology shops are everywhere.

cold-plunge.how: Cold Plunge SG on Neil Road and The Ice Bath Club offer ice baths.

running-club.how: Free clubs such as Running Department CBD sessions and Singapore Runners Club hold weekly runs.

animal-shelter-volunteering.how: Action for Singapore Dogs and SOSD let volunteers walk and socialise dogs.

pet-adoption.how: SPCA's adoption centre rehomes cats and dogs.

dog-parks.how: Dog runs inside NParks parks, e.g. Bishan Park and Punggol Waterway Park.
dog-parks.venue: Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park dog run

parkour.how: A2 Movements runs beginner parkour classes (trial classes listed).

urban-exploration.how: Most abandoned sites are government property so solo exploration risks trespass; guided tours of off-limits sites exist.
urban-exploration.venue: Hidden Heritage / Beyond Expeditions guided tours

meetups.how: Meetup hosts groups such as Silent Book Club Singapore.

coastal-cleanup.how: Volunteer coastal clean-ups run regularly; not verified here.

hot-spring-bathing.how: The Sembawang Hot Spring Park is a real geothermal spring, but bathing in pools is limited to foot soaks.

3d-printing.how: Makerspace@NDC (Fablab OMG) lists 3D printing among its capabilities; membership/day-pass terms not confirmed.

laser-cutting.how: Fablab OMG at Makerspace@NDC lists laser cutting; other makerspaces (RP, SMU-X) are mostly restricted to their own communities.

hackerspace-electronics.how: HackerspaceSG is a not-for-profit community space running meetups, workshops and member co-working with tools such as a 3D printer.

robotics-arduino.how: Tertiary Robotics sells kits and runs beginner robotics classes (price on enquiry; adult availability unconfirmed); one-off adult Arduino workshops have run at Lifelong Learning Institute.

amateur-radio.how: SARTS is the national amateur radio society with associate membership open to people without a licence; licensing is separate.

model-rocketry.how: University student rocketry societies (Singapore Propulsion Labs, SEDS Singapore) build rockets but launches happen overseas (e.g. California, New Mexico); no public launch site found.

ctf-security.how: Government and industry run CTFs (GovTech STACK the Flags, CSIT TISC at DEF CON Singapore, PwC Hackathon Challenge); some are student-only.
ctf-security.venue: DEF CON Singapore / GovTech STACK the Flags

hackathons.how: Corporate and university hackathons run regularly, e.g. PwC Singapore Hackathon Challenge; many target students.

game-development-jams.how: Global Game Jam Singapore 2025 ran in person at MAGES Institute and online; Garena also ran a 2025 invite-based game jam.
game-development-jams.venue: MAGES Institute (Global Game Jam Singapore site)

coding-meetups.how: HackerspaceSG hosts regular events, presentations and workshops for tech communities.

cnc-machining.how: Institutional makerspaces such as Republic Polytechnic's let members of the public in only by enrolling in selected CET courses; CNC specifically not confirmed.

watchmaking-horology.how: Beginner studio sessions where you assemble a mechanical watch movement with a Swiss master watchmaker; brand boutiques (e.g. Jaeger-LeCoultre at Marina Bay Sands) also run masterclasses.

fireworks-pyrotechnics.how: Private fireworks and explosives are tightly regulated; only licensed professionals run displays, so hobby pyrotechnics is not legally possible.

chess.how: Singapore Chess Federation runs graded courses taught by FIDE trainers (mainly ages 6-14, adults can also join) and clubs like Bishan Chess Club.

go-weiqi.how: Singapore Weiqi Association has a clubhouse at Bishan CC (non-members pay a daily fee) and runs adult beginner classes.

mahjong.how: Mahjong Lah runs beginner and intermediate Singapore-mahjong sessions at Co. on Duxton Road; home-hosted lessons are also listed.
mahjong.venue: Mahjong Lah at Co., 99 Duxton Rd

board-games.how: Singapore has many board game cafes with large libraries, e.g. The Mind Cafe, Settlers Cafe, King and the Pawn.

dungeons-and-dragons.how: Dungeoneers Rest runs paid learn-to-play D&D sessions; Singapore Comic Con and organised-play groups also host tables.

contract-bridge.how: Tanglin Club runs three duplicate bridge sessions a week with a director (club members); Geylang West CC has a free bridge interest group via OnePA.

escape-rooms.how: Dozens of escape rooms island-wide, e.g. LOST SG at Bencoolen, Xcape, The Escape Artist, Black Lake Facility.

esports-gaming.how: EXP at Kallang Wave Mall is an esports centre with an open LAN area and event space (2021 source; current status not rechecked).
esports-gaming.venue: EXP Esports Experience Centre, Kallang Wave Mall

paintball.how: Crossfire Paintball at Singapore Discovery Centre and Red Dynasty at Turf City are listed paintball venues.

airsoft.how: TactSim at HomeTeamNS Khatib offers indoor player-vs-player airsoft with rented equipment; personal airsoft guns are tightly regulated.

larp.how: LARP Singapore Community runs events and sessions (18+); Ren Faire SG and LARP Battle SG have also run as one-off events.

poker.how: Poker is legal at the casinos (Resorts World Sentosa has a poker room; Marina Bay Sands mostly house-banked variants); home games only among friends at home, not for profit. Casino entry for locals is an extra hurdle (levy).

billiards-snooker.how: Lagoon Billiard Room at SAFRA Toa Payoh has 9 snooker and 8 American pool tables; Arena Billiards and Gallop Billiards are others.
billiards-snooker.venue: Lagoon Billiard Room, SAFRA Toa Payoh

ten-pin-bowling.how: SuperBowl operates bowling centres island-wide (Marina Square has 18 lanes); Orchid Bowl at The Chevrons in Boon Lay has 24.

pub-trivia.how: Weekly quiz nights at Irish and British pubs, e.g. Molly Malone's (Mondays), Prince of Wales, Penny Black; plus roaming SG Tipsy Trivia.
pub-trivia.venue: Molly Malone's Irish Pub, Circular Road

speedcubing.how: WCA-sanctioned competitions run several times a year, e.g. Mofunland Speedcubing Singapore 2026 (164 competitors).

wargaming-warhammer.how: Gamersaurus Rex is a hobby shop known as a meeting place for Warhammer 40K, Magic and D&D, with regular gaming nights.

trading-card-games.how: Grey Ogre Games (Club Street and Ann Siang Road) is a large MTG/TCG retailer with an events calendar; specific play events not verified.

arcade-games.how: Timezone runs arcades with VR and bowling at outlets such as Jurong Point and Chinatown Point.

vr-gaming.how: Timezone promotes VR games, and some escape rooms (The Escape Artist, Lockdown) have VR rooms.

cosplay.how: Singapore Comic Con at Sands Expo (5-6 Dec 2026) has a cosplay competition; LARP/Ren Faire events also welcome costumes.

hiking.how: Paved and forested ridge trail linking Mount Faber to Kent Ridge, about 9-10 km, with NParks guided walks also offered.

camping.how: Permit-based tent camping at designated campsites (Jelutong, Mamam, Endut Senin) on Pulau Ubin; other legal sites exist but are few.

stargazing.how: Light-polluted city, but Science Centre Observatory runs public telescope nights and amateurs hold star parties at East Coast Park; weather and haze limit it.

allotment-gardening.how: NParks leases small allotment plots in parks (ballot when oversubscribed); also community gardens via Community in Bloom.

intertidal-walking.how: Guided walks over the Chek Jawa intertidal flats at low spring tide; NParks tours reported suspended for maintenance and bookings are competitive.

orienteering.how: Park-based orienteering races and O-training run by the Orienteering Federation Singapore; mostly urban parks, no real forest. Sources are 2018-2019, so current activity unverified.

urban-foraging.how: Plant collecting is prohibited in nature reserves; the nearest legal version is a guided edible-plant foraging tour of rooftop farms in the City Hall area.
urban-foraging.venue: Edible Garden City (Raffles City / Funan urban farms)

freshwater-fishing.how: Rod fishing allowed in marked zones, e.g. the Jurong Lake recreational jetty (artificial bait only), plus free spots like the Changi boardwalk.

nature-guided-walks.how: Free NParks Nature Appreciation Walks at Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, about an hour, registration required.

mountain-biking.how: Ketam Mountain Bike Park and dirt trails on Pulau Ubin; bikes rentable at the jetty (some rentals bar the Ketam trails).

trail-running.how: Compacted forest trails around MacRitchie Reservoir (about 11 km loop) and the Rail Corridor.

treetop-walk.how: 250 m suspension bridge about 25 m above the forest floor in MacRitchie, reached by a long forest trail; opening days vary by source.

hydroponics-urban-farming.how: Hands-on tabletop hydroponics workshops at a high-tech vertical farm; also rooftop farm tours and volunteer sessions (ComCrop).

outdoor-rock-climbing.how: Few natural crags in Singapore; climbing is almost entirely indoors at dozens of bouldering and wall gyms (e.g. Climb Central, Onsight).

mushroom-foraging.how: Removing plants, fungi or animals from parks and nature reserves is prohibited, and there is no seasonal forest-foraging culture.

birds-of-prey-watching.how: Migratory raptors pass through Sept-April and peregrine falcons are seen on tall buildings; NParks biodiversity pages document them.

meteorite-hunting.how: No desert or ice fields to search; meteorites are only in museum or dealer hands.

indoor-skydiving.how: Vertical wind tunnel in Sentosa: briefing plus two short flights with an instructor; simulated, not a real jump.

bungee-jumping.how: About 50 m tower on Siloso Beach with a few seconds of freefall and optional pool dip.

outdoor-skydiving.how: No drop zone for civilian skydiving was found in Singapore; real jumps are overseas (e.g. Malaysia, Thailand, New Zealand).

base-jumping.how: No cliffs or structures that can legally be jumped, and airspace and building rules are strict.

snow-skiing.how: Tropical climate with no natural snow; nearest real slopes are in Japan or Korea.

ski-simulator.how: Indoor conveyor-style ski/snowboard simulator with coach-led lessons (listed at the EU Holidays Expo, Raffles Boulevard).

indoor-snow-play.how: Snow City, the indoor snow centre near Science Centre, was reported (Wikipedia) to close on 30 Sep 2026; closure not confirmed on operator site, recheck.

hunting.how: Hunting wildlife is illegal and there is no huntable land.

safari.how: No wild big game, but the Night Safari and Singapore Zoo offer a captive-wildlife tram and walking experience.

zip-lining.how: MegaZip drops about 450 m from Imbiah Hill toward Siloso Beach at around 60 km/h.

luge.how: Wheeled gravity cart luge on four tracks at Sentosa's Imbiah Lookout, not an ice luge.

cable-wakeboarding.how: Cable-ski lagoon with beginner-friendly cable systems for wakeboarding and water-skiing, gear included.

cave-exploring.how: No natural cave systems or karst; only WWII tunnels with no public caving.

cave-diving.how: No flooded caves; nearest cave-diving sites are in Malaysia, Mexico or Florida.

glacier-trekking.how: No glaciers or ice fields within thousands of kilometres.

volcano-boarding.how: No volcanoes in Singapore; nearest are in Indonesia.

bullfighting.how: No bullfighting or bull-running tradition, and animal-cruelty laws would prohibit it.

rodeo.how: No rodeo circuit or livestock culture in Singapore.

paragliding.how: No suitable hills or flight clearance; flying sites are in Malaysia and elsewhere.

hot-air-ballooning.how: No balloon operators; dense airspace around Changi, Paya Lebar and Seletar bars it.

white-water-rafting.how: No rivers with rapids; nearest rafting is in Malaysia.

canyoning.how: No canyons or gorges in Singapore.

sandboarding-desert.how: No dunes or desert; only beach sand.

high-ropes-course.how: Multi-level aerial obstacle courses at Mega Adventure Park (Sentosa); specific course not verified.

clay-shooting.how: Licensed clubs such as SAFRA Shooting Club and Singapore Gun Club offer trap/skeet but access is limited; laser clay shooting is the open alternative.
clay-shooting.venue: SAFRA Shooting Club / Singapore Gun Club

mountaineering.how: Highest point is Bukit Timah Hill (163 m); real mountaineering needs trips to Malaysia, Nepal or beyond, though climbing gyms help training.

ballet.how: Singapore Ballet runs term-based adult beginner classes (no prior experience needed).

salsa-bachata.how: Many studios offer cheap trial classes in salsa, bachata and kizomba; no partner needed.

flamenco.how: Los Tarantos (Singapore Flamenco Club, NAFA) and Spanish Dance Singapore teach flamenco at all levels.

bharatanatyam.how: SIFAS and Apsaras Arts teach this Indian classical dance from beginner to advanced; LASALLE ran an adult short course.

lion-dance.how: Clan and athletic associations run lion dance troupes with beginner training in drumming and footwork; Chinatown has run public workshops.
lion-dance.venue: Chin Woo Athletic Association lion dance troupe

kathak.how: SIFAS teaches Kathak; Apsaras Arts has also run Kathak classes.

swing-lindy-hop.how: SwingStation teaches Lindy Hop levels 1-3 at Aliwal Arts Centre; Jitterbugs Swingapore also offers it.

breakdancing.how: EV Dance and Kulture Studios run hip-hop and b-boy classes; SCAPE has hosted breaking intensives.

tango.how: A weekly beginner Argentine tango group class runs on Wednesdays at Allenby House; no partner needed.

irish-dance.how: Irish Inspirational Dance is a Singapore school with an adult class, listed by the Irish Embassy.

malay-dance.how: Sri Warisan Som Said runs public Malay dance workshops (inang, asli, zapin, joget), e.g. at the Singapore Heritage Festival; regular classes unverified.
malay-dance.venue: Sri Warisan Som Said Performing Arts

pole-dance.how: Several dedicated studios (The Brass Barre, SLAP, PXD) offer pole classes with cheap trials.

tap-dance.how: Adult beginner tap classes are listed in Bugis, and Tanglin Arts Studio teaches tap among other genres.

aerial-silks-circus.how: Circus Swingapore and Aerial Fitness Studio teach silks, lyra and static trapeze to beginners.

piano.how: Dozens of private studios and music schools teach adult piano.

guitar.how: Many music schools and private teachers offer guitar lessons.

guzheng.how: Eason Music School and other Chinese music schools offer guzheng group and private lessons.

erhu.how: Eason Music School teaches erhu privately; People's Association community centres run 10-session adult erhu courses that can lead into community Chinese orchestras.
erhu.venue: People's Association community centre courses (ONE PA)

sitar.how: SIFAS is cited by NLB as offering sitar lessons; current class status not confirmed.

tabla.how: SIFAS has a resident tabla guru (Supriyo Banerjee); enrolment requires SIFAS membership.

gamelan.how: Gamelan is mostly played in school/polytechnic CCAs; NUS Singa Nglaras Gamelan Ensemble also accepts outside members.

bagpipes.how: Pipe bands exist in schools (ACS Independent Boys' Brigade, Northland Secondary) and the Women Police Pipes and Drums Band; public lessons not confirmed.

harp.how: Rave Harps Academy and private teachers (listed on harpcenter) teach harp; NAFA and NUS YST Conservatory have harp programmes.

taiko.how: HIBIKIYA and Mangrove Learning (formerly School of Daiko) teach taiko, including adult courses via ONE PA.

choir.how: Non-auditioned adult choirs such as VOS Chorus of the People and Vox Camerata welcome beginners.

orchestra.how: Volunteer orchestras like Braddell Heights Symphony Orchestra, Orchestra of the Music Makers and The Philharmonic Orchestra recruit amateur players.

chinese-orchestra.how: Community Chinese orchestras (e.g. Keat Hong Chinese Orchestra) run under community clubs, and ONE PA erhu courses feed into them.

improv-comedy.how: The Improv Company, founded 2013, is Singapore's improv school and runs beginner courses.

stand-up-comedy.how: Weekly open mics (Talk Cock Comedy at Blu Jaz Cafe) and short beginner courses like Grab the Mic let novices perform.
stand-up-comedy.venue: Blu Jaz Cafe (Talk Cock Comedy open mic)

magic.how: Republic Polytechnic's magic group runs workshops for amateurs; IBM Singapore Ring 115 is the local society; adult classes were not confirmed.

dj-turntablism.how: Zouk Academy, E-TracX DJ Skool and Show Ning DJ School teach DJing on Pioneer decks; equipment can be rented.

music-production.how: Ableton Certified Trainers (Ben Ang, Syafiq Halid) and Garnish Music Production teach production; NUS Electronic Music Lab also exists.

chinese-opera.how: Singapore Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan ran 10-week Teochew opera singing classes; Nam Hwa Opera trains children and adults.
chinese-opera.venue: Singapore Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan

acting.how: Time Out lists several acting classes and workshops for adults in Singapore.

bouldering.how: Dedicated bouldering gyms run beginner classes and rent shoes.

rock-climbing-top-rope.how: Tall indoor walls with top-rope and auto-belay lanes, plus boulder areas.

big-wall-climbing.how: No natural big walls exist on the island; indoor walls top out around 16 m, and real big-wall climbing means travelling abroad.

archery.how: Indoor ranges offer trial shoots and beginner courses.

fencing.how: Private clubs run beginner programmes in foil, epee and sabre.

ice-skating.how: Real-ice public rink with lessons for all levels; the older JCube rink closed in 2023.

ice-hockey.how: The Singapore Ice Hockey Association has run adult leagues (e.g. 2018 Lion City Cup at JCube) but the Olympic-size rink closed in 2023, so ice time is scarce.

curling.how: A curling lane at Kallang Ice World was reported by one source but not confirmed on an official page.

snowboarding.how: No snow or slopes in Singapore; must travel abroad.

ski-jumping.how: Requires a purpose-built hill and snow or plastic matting; none exists in Singapore.

bobsled.how: Needs an ice track; none in Singapore.

skateboarding.how: Large free public skate parks, including Singapore's biggest outdoor skate park.

bmx.how: Free BMX riding at the Xtreme SkatePark and a UCI-certified BMX track at Tampines Bike Park.

disc-golf.how: Free permanent 18-hole course at Tanglin Hill plus a 10-hole course at Kallang Riverside Park and pop-up courses.

ultimate-frisbee.how: Community club Chuckies, university teams and pick-up games; the national mixed team reached world finals in 2023.

gaelic-football-hurling.how: Singapore Gaelic Lions play Gaelic football, hurling and camogie.

australian-rules-football.how: ANZA Wombats and Wombettes train at Centaurs Sports Fields, Turf City; everyone welcome per club site.

lawn-bowls.how: Bowls Singapore runs sessions at Sports Hub, Boon Lay and Tampines, with a discover-lawn-bowls programme.

horse-riding.how: Bukit Timah Saddle Club offers beginner lessons to non-members; it relocated to Kranji after its old site closed in 2023.

horse-polo.how: Singapore Polo Club offers lessons; Colts Polo & Riding teaches at the Turf Club riding centre in Kranji.

elephant-polo.how: Needs working elephants; none are kept for sport in Singapore. Played in Nepal, Thailand and India.

camel-racing.how: No camel racing in Singapore; found in the Gulf states and Australia.

buzkashi.how: Central Asian horseback game needing a trained horse culture and open steppe; none in Singapore.

taekwondo.how: ActiveSG Academy runs beginner taekwondo for ages 13 and up.

silat.how: Singapore Silat Federation runs classes; location by enquiry.

judo.how: Singapore Judo Club is one of the oldest dojos in the country.

capoeira.how: Several schools teach beginners, with a $10 trial at Xango Capoeira.

sepak-takraw.how: Singapore Sepaktakraw Federation has 21 affiliated clubs; also played in schools.

netball.how: Netball Super League and community play exist in Singapore.

lacrosse.how: Singapore Lacrosse Association holds practices and scrimmages (reported at Farrer Park).

pickleball.how: Indoor air-conditioned and outdoor courts bookable by the hour.
pickleball.venue: SPH Pickle Padel at Singapore Expo

padel.how: Several padel courts bookable via Playtomic.

drone-racing.how: FPV coaching and club flights exist, school competitions run, but about three quarters of Singapore is no-fly zone and there is no recurring public race league.

dinghy-sailing.how: Changi Sailing Club rents dinghies and keelboats; the Singapore Sailing Federation's ActiveSailing runs intro courses.

cricket.how: Singapore Cricket Club at the Padang fields cricket sides; other leagues exist.

rugby.how: Singapore Rugby Union and clubs such as the Singapore Cricket Club field rugby sides.

dragon-boat.how: Beginner dragon boat sessions at Kallang by AustCham Paddle Club and other teams.
dragon-boat.venue: AustCham Paddle Club (Kallang Dragon Boat Nursery)

cheese-rolling.how: A single English hill event; no Singapore equivalent.

oil-painting.how: Studios run beginner oil painting trial classes and multi-session courses with all materials supplied.

watercolour-painting.how: Watercolour landscape masterclasses and workshops are offered by Visual Arts Centre and shophouse studios like Artify.

chinese-ink-painting.how: Weekly evening classes and trial workshops teach the four gentlemen then birds-and-flowers and landscape.

charcoal-life-drawing.how: Guided and open life drawing sessions with live models run at art studios and galleries.
charcoal-life-drawing.venue: Chalk N Pencils (New Bahru) / Maya Gallery

urban-sketching.how: Urban Sketchers Singapore holds free monthly sketchwalks at different places on the island.

pottery-wheel.how: Many studios offer one-off wheel throwing taster classes with glazing and firing included.

pottery-handbuilding.how: Family-run Thow Kwang Pottery Jungle (since 1965) offers hand-building sessions with firing in its kiln.

glassblowing.how: Tombalek runs beginner hot-shop glassblowing classes at Singapore's only public glass melting furnace; glass artist B. Jane Cowie also teaches.

lampworking.how: Short beginner flameworking sessions make small glass pieces like mini bouquets.

stained-glass.how: Small-group suncatcher workshops teach cutting, grinding, foiling and soldering.
stained-glass.venue: Felicia Yong stained glass workshop (via Pelago)

blacksmithing.how: Tombalek is listed as teaching blacksmithing and a bladesmithing workshop for forging a knife; schedules were not confirmed.

leatherwork.how: Studios in Haji Lane and elsewhere run wallet and cardholder workshops with vegetable-tanned leather and tools provided.

woodworking.how: Beginner workshops build a side table or memory box in small groups with tools and safety briefing.

weaving.how: Beginner frame-loom wall hanging classes and Saori freestyle weaving sessions are offered.

batik-painting.how: Two-hour batik painting workshops with Singapore motifs run weekly; tjanting wax-resist workshops also exist.

printmaking-screenprint.how: STPI runs beginner printmaking workshops combining screenprint, etching and relief; National Gallery hosted screenprint sessions with STPI.

etching.how: STPI's Print Fusion workshop included acid-etching copper plates; regular dedicated etching courses were not confirmed.

lithography.how: STPI is a professional lithography workshop and has offered lithography stations at open events; no regular public course confirmed.

bookbinding.how: Objectifs teaches dos-a-dos, pamphlet and link-stitch binding; Based Book Arts runs Coptic and link-stitch workshops.
bookbinding.venue: Objectifs Centre for Photography and Film

perfumery.how: Several studios run guided custom-perfume blending sessions, e.g. Oo La Lab in Chinatown.

candle-making.how: Small-group scented soy and decorative candle workshops are widely offered.

knitting-crochet.how: Beginner crochet classes run inside craft stores and via community centres; yarn shops cluster at People's Park.

embroidery.how: Drop-in beginner embroidery workshops with materials provided are run daily by studios.

peranakan-beadwork.how: A 2-hour Nonya beading workshop for beginners has been run with the Peranakan Museum community.

origami.how: Free or occasional origami sessions exist (Family Central course; Japan Creative Centre workshops) but no regular paid adult classes were found.

ikebana.how: Ikebana International Singapore Chapter 135 (since 1969) holds public workshops and members teach Ikenobo, Sogetsu and Ohara schools.

jewellery-silversmithing.how: 3-hour beginner silversmithing workshops in a Joo Chiat heritage space; ring-making studios in Orchard.
jewellery-silversmithing.venue: Silversmithing workshop at 229 Joo Chiat Rd

clay-sculpture.how: LASALLE's continuing education offers an 8-session Sculpture I clay course.
clay-sculpture.venue: LASALLE College of the Arts (via C3A listing)

stone-carving.how: Sculpture Society Singapore ran a six-lesson stone carving masterclass in 2018; no current public class confirmed.

photography.how: Objectifs runs a 6-session Foundational Photography Workshop for beginners; limited loan cameras.
photography.venue: Objectifs Centre for Photography and Film

film-photography-darkroom.how: Objectifs' Black & White I workshop teaches shooting film and developing prints in its darkroom.
film-photography-darkroom.venue: Objectifs Centre for Photography and Film

filmmaking.how: Objectifs' Digital Filmmaking workshop covers scripting through editing for beginners, with cameras supplied.
filmmaking.venue: Objectifs Centre for Photography and Film

animation-2d.how: LASALLE offers an Introduction to 2D Animation short course using Krita; open to anyone interested.

tattooing.how: Tattoo artists learn via apprenticeships at studios; a fake-skin 'pseudo tattoo' workshop exists for a taste, and it certifies no one.

kintsugi.how: Several studios teach modern kintsugi repair with resin and gold powder on pottery.

rug-tufting.how: Dedicated tufting studios like WeTuft run walk-in and multi-hour rug tufting sessions.

macrame.how: A 3-hour beginner macrame wall hanging class runs in a Thomson Green home studio with materials provided.
macrame.venue: Macrame wall hanging workshop (via Seek Sophie)

snow-sculpture.how: Natural snow does not exist in the tropics; real snow sculpting means travelling to places like Sapporo or Harbin.

sailing.how: Changi Sailing Club runs public beginner sailing courses.

keelboat-yachting.how: One15 Marina Club in Sentosa Cove offers sailing courses to members and non-members.

kayaking.how: Rent single kayaks by the 2-hour block on the Kallang Basin; no licence needed.
kayaking.venue: Singapore Sports Hub Water Sports Centre

mangrove-sea-kayaking.how: Guided kayak tours through Pulau Ubin mangroves, reached by bumboat from Changi Point.

stand-up-paddleboarding.how: SUP lessons and board hire at Sentosa's Tanjong Beach.

sup-yoga.how: SUP Yoga Singapore runs lessons at Mana Mana Beach Club.
sup-yoga.venue: Mana Mana Beach Club (SUP Yoga Singapore)

windsurfing.how: Constant Wind at NSRCC Changi runs windsurfing courses; East Coast Park also has schools.

kitesurfing.how: Lessons are advertised at East Coast Park, but light and unreliable wind limits sessions.
kitesurfing.venue: Mana Mana Beach Club (Windsurfing, Kitesurfing & SUP school)

scuba-diving.how: PADI courses and fun dives at Pulau Hantu; visibility is often only 2-3 m.

freediving.how: Freedive SG / Singapore Freediving Academy runs multi-agency freediving courses.

snorkeling.how: Snorkel off Lazarus, Kusu and Hantu islands; visibility is usually under 5 m.

wakeboarding.how: Cable-park wakeboarding with instructors on a beginner cable system.

cable-skiing.how: Singapore Wake Park is the country's cable-ski park, with three cable systems.

water-skiing.how: Done on the cable systems at Singapore Wake Park rather than behind a boat.

surfing-ocean.how: Singapore's sheltered straits have no rideable surf; people travel to Malaysia, Indonesia or Bali.

surf-simulator.how: Wave House Sentosa (the FlowRider venue) closed in October 2019; no replacement was found.

outrigger-canoe.how: AustCham Paddle Club also runs outrigger canoe paddling out of Marina Bay.

pedal-boating.how: PAssion WaVe at Marina Bay hires pedal boats, bell boats and kayaks.

rowing.how: Singapore Rowing Association runs a Learn-to-Row course: ergometer basics then quad boat on water.

fishing.how: Free shore fishing at designated grounds such as Kranji Reservoir Park; no licence for angling.

fishing-pond.how: Pay-per-session saltwater fishing pond at Pasir Ris Town Park.

drone-flying.how: Open fields designated for uncrewed aircraft, e.g. Pandan Reservoir; drones over 250g must be registered.

rc-aircraft.how: Flying fields exist but are scarce; no public club field was confirmed.

control-line-aeromodelling.how: Mostly via school Singapore Youth Flying Club CCAs; no clear public club found.

hang-gliding.how: No suitable terrain or airspace; people go to Malaysia or Thailand.

kite-flying.how: Open lawns such as Marina Barrage are popular for flying kites.

bmx.how: Po Kong Village Road Park was built for BMX and the Tseung Kwan O velodrome skatepark takes freestyle BMX.

bobsled.how: Needs a purpose-built ice track; none in Hong Kong (nearest in South Korea or Japan, a few hours by air).

bouldering.how: Several bouldering gyms including Just Climb and n bouldering run beginner classes.

buzkashi.how: Central Asian horseback game with no tradition or venue in Hong Kong.

camel-racing.how: No camel racing in Hong Kong; found in the Gulf states, Australia and Mongolia.

cheese-rolling.how: A single annual English hill event with no Hong Kong equivalent.

cricket.how: Hong Kong Cricket Club has turf and astro nets and an indoor three-lane cricket centre; other clubs also field sides.

dinghy-sailing.how: LCSD water sports centres at Stanley, St Stephen's Beach, Tai Mei Tuk, Chong Hing and Wong Shek run sailing courses.
dinghy-sailing.venue: Stanley Main Beach Water Sports Centre

elephant-polo.how: Needs trained elephants; held in Thailand and Nepal, not in Hong Kong.

fencing.how: Union Fencing Club runs beginner fencing courses for children and adults on Hong Kong Island and in Kowloon.
fencing.source_url: https://kuddo.io/centre/Union Fencing Club - Children and Adult Fencing Courses in Hong Kong/5f4d23e6c2aea05c20367f80

horse-riding.how: Jockey Club public riding schools and private centres such as Clearwater Bay Equestrian Centre give lessons; Pok Fu Lam Public Riding School was being rebuilt with reopening status unclear.

ice-hockey.how: Penguins Hockey Club at Mega Ice runs classes for ages 5 to adult, and Mega Ice hosts an annual Hockey 5's tournament.

ice-skating.how: Mega Ice at MegaBox is the Olympic-sized public rink, with public sessions and figure skating courses.

rock-climbing-top-rope.how: Hong Kong Climbing Park in Sha Tin teaches beginner to intermediate classes on one of the city's largest walls.

judo.how: Judo classes for kids and beginners are listed at Kowloon Jiu-Jitsu in Tsim Sha Tsui.

lawn-bowls.how: Hong Kong Cricket Club has a lawn bowls green among its facilities (members and guests).

netball.how: The Hong Kong Netball League runs October-April leagues for adults and children; Hong Kong Cricket Club lists netball among its sports.

padel.how: Padel courts are mostly at private clubs (e.g. Hong Kong Country Club, Aberdeen Marina Club) that are members/guests only, so public access is limited.

pickleball.how: Hong Kong Football Club's Pickleball Interest Group meets in its indoor sports hall with a Sunday social session; 12+ public venues also exist.

rugby.how: Hong Kong Football Club fields rugby sides and hosts matches at its Happy Valley stadium.

skateboarding.how: Many public skateparks (Lai Chi Kok, Po Kong Village Road, Tseung Kwan O) plus the indoor Sk85ive2 park in Kwun Tong.

ski-jumping.how: Needs a snow-covered ski-jump hill; none in Hong Kong (nearest in Japan, about 4 hours by air).

snowboarding.how: Real-snow snowboarding is impossible in Hong Kong's subtropical climate; nearest slopes are in Japan or northern China, about 4 hours by air.

taekwondo.how: Family-oriented taekwondo schools run classes for all ages, e.g. U&I Korea Taekwondo in Wong Chuk Hang.

ultimate-frisbee.how: Ultimate is played in organised local leagues and pick-up sessions, per Sassy Mama's overview of trending sports.

dragon-boat.how: Stanley and other clubs paddle year-round, and the Hong Kong Dragon Boat Racing Association and clubs run beginner courses.

freediving.how: Sai Kung Scuba lists PADI freediving among its courses and Sai Kung waters are used for beginner freediving.

kayaking.how: Sea Kayak Hong Kong, Blue Sky Sports Club and Kayak Hong Kong run tours and rentals around Sai Kung and Cheung Chau.

sailing.how: Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club (Kellett Island, Shelter Cove) and LCSD water sports centres offer sailing.

scuba-diving.how: PADI centres such as Sai Kung Scuba and Diving Adventure run Open Water courses with dives around Sai Kung.

snorkeling.how: Snorkelling at Hoi Ha Wan Marine Park and Sharp Island, reachable from Sai Kung, with PADI snorkelling courses available.

stand-up-paddleboarding.how: SUP lessons and rentals at Sha Ha Beach in Sai Kung (HKSUPBA), Surf Hong Kong and Cheung Chau.
stand-up-paddleboarding.venue: Hong Kong Surf and Stand Up Paddle Board Association

surfing-ocean.how: Small beach-break waves at Big Wave Bay (Shek O) and Tai Long Wan in Sai Kung, with schools such as Surf Hong Kong; best from October to April.

wakeboarding.how: Hong Kong Wakeboard runs boat-towed wakeboarding at Tai Tam Tuk Reservoir.

windsurfing.how: Hiwindlover at Stanley Beach and Cheung Chau Windsurfing Centre offer lessons and rental; LCSD centres also teach windsurfing.

bullfighting.how: Bullfighting is not practised in Hong Kong; found in Spain, Portugal and Latin America.

dog-sledding.how: Needs snow and sled dogs; not possible in Hong Kong's climate (nearest in northern China or Japan).

glacier-trekking.how: No glaciers anywhere near Hong Kong; nearest are in the Himalaya or New Zealand, a day or more of travel.

high-ropes-course.how: XVENTURE indoor hub at Kornhill Plaza has the city's tallest indoor high-ropes course (about 3 m).

paragliding.how: Government-regulated sport with designated sites at Dragon's Back (Shek O), Sai Kung and South Lantau; Hong Kong Hike 'N' Fly offers tandem flights.

rodeo.how: No rodeo or bull-riding culture in Hong Kong; found in North America and Australia.

safari.how: No free-roaming large wildlife in Hong Kong; nearest safaris are in Southeast Asia or Africa.

sandboarding-desert.how: No desert terrain in Hong Kong; nearest dunes are in inland China.

snow-skiing.how: Real-snow skiing is impossible in Hong Kong's subtropical climate; nearest slopes are in Japan or northern China, about 4 hours by air.

volcano-boarding.how: No suitable volcano near Hong Kong; done on Cerro Negro in Nicaragua.

zip-lining.how: XVENTURE has a low ground-level indoor zip line and a Victoria Peak via ferrata package includes a zipline over the harbour; large outdoor ziplines are not yet open.

camping.how: AFCD runs 41 designated campsites in country parks, free and first come first served, with tables, toilets and barbecue pits.
camping.venue: Ham Tin Campsite (Sai Kung East Country Park)

hiking.how: The 50 km Hong Kong Trail runs along Hong Kong Island's ridges from the Peak to Shek O, one of many marked country park trails.

trail-running.how: The 100 km MacLehose Trail hosts ultra races such as the Hong Kong 100 and Oxfam Trailwalker, and the country park trails are used year-round by runners.

mountain-biking.how: Designated trails at Chi Ma Wan on Lantau (with a new practice ground at Mui Wo) and others in country parks.
mountain-biking.venue: Chi Ma Wan mountain bike trails

outdoor-rock-climbing.how: Trad, sport and bouldering routes on the Shek O sea cliffs, with a bigger sport-climbing crag at Tung Lung Chau reached by boat.

birdwatching.how: Hong Kong Birdwatching Society runs guided tours of the Mai Po wetland reserve; WWF also runs public eco-visits.

nature-guided-walks.how: AFCD runs free weekend guided ecotours at Hoi Ha Wan Marine Park (two sessions of up to 25 people), plus a self-guided leaflet.
nature-guided-walks.venue: Hoi Ha Wan Marine Park Visitor Centre

intertidal-walking.how: Corals can be viewed from the pier at low tide at Hoi Ha Wan, with guided ecotours on weekends; formal intertidal shore walks are limited.

stargazing.how: The free, 24-hour Astropark in Sai Kung has naked-eye and telescope observation areas, run by the Hong Kong Space Museum.

meteorite-hunting.how: No meteorite strewn fields or suitable desert terrain exist in Hong Kong; hunting means travelling to arid regions such as inland China or Australia.

snow-sculpture.how: Hong Kong has no natural snow; snow sculpture means travelling to northern China (Harbin) or Japan (Sapporo), several hours by air.

tango.how: Trio Spin Studio teaches tango from elementary to advanced levels.

flamenco.how: Trio Spin Studio also teaches flamenco alongside tango and salsa.

salsa-bachata.how: Dancetrinity runs salsa and bachata classes on a walk-in basis most nights.

ballet.how: Dancetrinity lists adult ballet classes among its walk-in programme.

pole-dance.how: Flaunt Studio teaches pole from beginner level through inverts and choreography; other studios exist in Cheung Sha Wan and Kwun Tong.

stand-up-comedy.how: Weekly English-language open mic comedy nights at Bar 109, with other bars in Central also hosting open mics.

improv-comedy.how: TakeOut Comedy Club has hosted improv shows, but a guide notes shows were limited to private or member events at the time of writing.

lion-dance.how: HKUST offers a beginner lion dance skill class (English with Cantonese support), but it is a university course; troupes perform citywide.
lion-dance.venue: HKUST Traditional Lion Dance for Beginners

dj-turntablism.how: Garnish Music Production runs a turntablism course in small classes of up to four, taught by a Red Bull Thre3style champion.

music-production.how: Garnish Music Production teaches production courses; VTC and HKCT also run full-time diplomas.

guzheng.how: The Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra runs music courses and youth zheng ensembles; adult guzheng instruction is not confirmed on the page.

pottery-wheel.how: Hong Kong Arts School (HKAC) runs 8-lesson beginner wheel-throwing courses; Lai Chan Kee and others offer one-off trial sessions.
pottery-wheel.venue: Hong Kong Arts School (Hong Kong Arts Centre)

leatherwork.how: motto in San Po Kong runs leather workshops from about 2 hours to 30 hours where participants stitch their own item.

candle-making.how: BeCandle in Sai Kung offers a weekend bespoke candle experience where visitors blend a scent and pour their own candle.

jewellery-silversmithing.how: PMQ has hosted silver jewellery masterclasses and the Hong Kong Palace Museum ran a silver pendant workshop; schedules are periodic.

glassblowing.how: PolyU continuing education has offered one-day glassblowing workshops at Jockey Club Creative Arts Centre; the studio Kaleidoscope also ran courses.
glassblowing.venue: Jockey Club Creative Arts Centre (PolyU glassblowing workshop)

bookbinding.how: Percy So, a Hong Kong fine bookbinder, has run private three-hour adult bookbinding workshops.
bookbinding.venue: Percy So bookbinding workshop (Harvard Club of Hong Kong listing)

etching.how: HKUST's printshop has held copper etching workshops, but this is a university programme.

trading-cards.how: Hong Kong has a large trading-card scene, with dedicated card shops and the Grade10 collector festival drawing record crowds.

3d-printing.how: Open-access fab lab in Sham Shui Po with a 3D printer and laser cutter for makers.

ctf-security.how: HKCERT runs an annual Capture the Flag challenge (mostly online, with an on-site final), so it is a yearly event rather than a regular club activity.

coding-meetups.how: Hong Kong Python User Group and Open Source Hong Kong hold free in-person meetups roughly every month or two.
coding-meetups.venue: Hong Kong Python User Group / Open Source Hong Kong

hackerspace-electronics.how: Dim Sum Labs is the city's long-running hackerspace with open nights for electronics and fabrication.

fireworks-pyrotechnics.how: Hobby fireworks making is effectively unavailable: manufacture and handling of fireworks fall under dangerous-goods licensing and displays are run only by licensed operators; nearest hobby scene is across the border in mainland China.

laser-cutting.how: Laser cutter access at a Sham Shui Po fab lab.

board-games.how: Board-game cafes with hundreds of titles and staff who teach the rules.

ten-pin-bowling.how: Large bowling centre with 40 lanes plus pool tables and karaoke.

go-weiqi.how: The Hong Kong Go Association (founded 1982) organises training, ranking and tournaments for Go players.

contract-bridge.how: The Hong Kong, China Contract Bridge Association is an SF&OC member and runs club and international events.

dungeons-and-dragons.how: Hong Kong Tabletop Gaming Group runs weekly drop-in D&D and one-shot RPG sessions (English and Chinese).
dungeons-and-dragons.venue: Hong Kong Tabletop Gaming Group (One-Shot Saturday)

escape-rooms.how: Themed physical escape rooms with 45-minute games.

esports-gaming.how: The 25,000 sq ft Cyber Games Arena has an 80-person arena, training facilities and high-end gaming PCs, and hosts competitions.

mahjong.how: Beginner Hong Kong-style mahjong classes, with an optional outing to a mahjong parlour.
mahjong.venue: American Women's Association of Hong Kong

pub-trivia.how: Many bars host weekly quiz nights, e.g. Delaney's in Wan Chai on Wednesdays.

speedcubing.how: The Hong Kong Rubik's Cube Union organises one or two WCA-sanctioned competitions a year (e.g. Hong Kong Cube Day, The Wave, Kwun Tong).
speedcubing.venue: Hong Kong Rubik's Cube Union (Hong Kong Cube Day)

vr-gaming.how: Walk-in VR arcades with HTC Vive rigs and an omni-directional treadmill.

beekeeping-honey.how: Kadoorie Farm runs an annual beekeeping course on native bees for honey production (taught in Cantonese).

homebrewing-beer.how: Three-hour hands-on homebrewing workshop where participants brew a batch.

mixology.how: HKU SPACE runs a 30-hour cocktail appreciation and mixology certificate with hands-on crafting and a bar visit.
mixology.venue: HKU SPACE (F&B Education Hub, Kowloon West Campus)

coffee-roasting.how: YMCA of Hong Kong's barista academy lists short courses including Roasting for Beginners with hands-on roasting.
coffee-roasting.venue: YMCA of Hong Kong Barista Training Academy

latte-art.how: HKU SPACE offers a specialty coffee programme covering espresso, milk texturing and latte art with SCA certification.
latte-art.venue: HKU SPACE (F&B Education Hub, Kowloon West Campus)

dim-sum-making.how: Private Cantonese dim sum classes in English with a chef, ending with a shared meal.
dim-sum-making.venue: Cookly (Yau Ma Tei dim sum class)

pasta-and-general-cooking-classes.how: Several cooking schools run hands-on classes, including Yum Cha and ABC Cooking Studio.

hawker-crawling.how: Cooked food centres and the remaining dai pai dong street stalls are the city's equivalent of hawker centres.
hawker-crawling.venue: Tai Po Market Cooked Food Centre

tea-ceremony.how: The Chado Urasenke Tankokai Hong Kong Association teaches and demonstrates tea ceremony, mainly for group or institutional bookings (Yuko-an tea room at CityU).
tea-ceremony.venue: Yuko-an Urasenke tea room, City University of Hong Kong

sake-tasting.how: WSET Level 1 Award in Sake (about 9 contact hours with tasting and food pairing) is offered through HKU SPACE.

sushi-making.how: Small-group sushi classes with local chefs.

whisky-tasting.how: HKU SPACE runs a world whisky appreciation certificate tasting dozens of whiskies, plus spirits courses.

wine-tasting-wset.how: HKU SPACE offers wine tasting and WSET certificate courses.

archival-research.how: The Public Records Office holds the government archives with a public reading service and online catalogue.

art-gallery.how: M+ is a major visual culture museum at West Kowloon, alongside Tai Kwun and commercial galleries.

creative-writing.how: Hong Kong Public Libraries runs writing workshops for novices (e.g. poetry, with the Hong Kong Poetry Association).

history-walks.how: University and commercial guided walks cover Central, Sheung Wan and Kowloon Walled City.

french-language.how: HKU SPACE is a leading adult provider of French courses.

german-language.how: HKU SPACE is a leading adult provider of German courses.

japanese-language.how: HKU SPACE is a leading adult provider of Japanese courses.

korean-language.how: HKU SPACE is a leading adult provider of Korean courses.

spanish-language.how: HKU SPACE is a leading adult provider of Spanish courses.

museums.how: Government and private museums include the Hong Kong Museum of History.

moocs.how: Global MOOC platforms are accessible from Hong Kong without restriction.

poetry-slam.how: Weekly open-mic poetry nights such as Peel Street Poetry in Central (listing dated 2016, status unconfirmed).

public-lectures.how: Hong Kong Public Libraries and the Science Museum host public talk series.

science-museum.how: A large government science museum with hands-on exhibits.

heritage-trails.how: Signposted heritage trails in the New Territories, such as the Ping Shan Heritage Trail.

toastmasters.how: Hong Kong Toastmasters Club is among several clubs in the city.

wartime-history.how: Museum of Coastal Defence in a former fort covers the 1941 Battle of Hong Kong.
wartime-history.venue: Hong Kong Museum of Coastal Defence

cold-plunge.how: A communal cold plunge club with a sauna and magnesium bath operates in Kennedy Town.

sauna.how: Finnish saunas with plunge tubs and contrast-therapy studios operate in Central and Wan Chai.

meetups.how: Meetup groups cover hobbies from tabletop gaming to coding.

hot-spring-bathing.how: No natural hot springs exist in Hong Kong; nearest are in Guangdong (a few hours away) or Japan.

pet-adoption.how: The SPCA runs a rescue and adoption programme for dogs and cats.

temple-activities.how: Working Taoist temples such as Man Mo Temple and Wong Tai Sin Temple welcome visitors and worshippers.

volunteering.how: Many charities and rescue groups recruit volunteers.

yoga.how: Dozens of studios; Pure Yoga has 12 locations.

big-wall-climbing.how: Hong Kong crags such as Tung Lung Chau and Lantau's Temple Crag offer multi-pitch trad and sport routes up to roughly 70 m, but there are no true big walls.

capoeira.how: Weekly drop-in capoeira classes run in Quarry Bay and at BeWater in Tsim Sha Tsui, alongside the Capoeira Federation of Hong Kong.
capoeira.venue: Quarry Bay Capoeira / BeWater Martial Arts & Wellness

hunting.how: Recreational hunting is not available: wild animals are protected by ordinance and there is no licensed sport-hunting scene; the nearest hunting is on the mainland.

drone-racing.how: Hong Kong FPV Racers, founded in 2015, organises FPV and nano drone racing; the Hong Kong Drone Sports Association ran an FAI-sanctioned open in 2019, and races need Civil Aviation Department permission.

freshwater-fishing.how: Reservoir angling is permitted at Plover Cove and other reservoirs from September to March with a Water Supplies Department licence.

geocaching.how: Geocaching has been active since the first cache in Lung Fu Shan Country Park in 2002, with caches in parks, hiking trails and urban areas.
geocaching.venue: Lung Fu Shan Country Park caches

birds-of-prey-watching.how: The Hong Kong Bird Watching Society runs raptor identification workshops and Mai Po tours targeting eagles, and migration season draws raptors over the territory.
birds-of-prey-watching.venue: Hong Kong Bird Watching Society / Mai Po Nature Reserve

hydroponics-urban-farming.how: K-FARM in Sheung Shui runs urban farming workshops covering hydroponics, aquaponics and organic rooftop farming.

urban-foraging.how: Guided foraging walks for edible and medicinal wild plants in the countryside have been led by local guides such as Wanda Huang, though not on a regular schedule.

cable-skiing.how: GO PARK Aqua at Sai Sha offers wakeboarding towed by an electric cable or boat, with full equipment rental.

fishing.how: Angling is possible from piers and reservoirs, and Kau Sai Wan Recreational Fishing Wonderland near Sai Kung offers a boat trip with gear and a crash course.
fishing.venue: Kau Sai Wan Recreational Fishing Wonderland

mangrove-sea-kayaking.how: Guided SUP and kayak tours of the Ting Kok mangroves in Tai Po are run by operators such as Holimood, and GO PARK Sai Sha schedules mangrove kayaking sessions.

hot-air-ballooning.how: Hong Kong has no regular balloon operation; the AIA International Hot Air Balloon Festival at the Central Harbourfront held tethered rides in September 2025 as a one-off event.
hot-air-ballooning.venue: AIA International Hot Air Balloon Festival

keelboat-yachting.how: Hebe Haven Yacht Club runs Hong Kong Sailing Federation-accredited keelboat courses on J/80 keelboats, open to non-members aged 16 and over.

kite-flying.how: Kite flying is allowed at designated spots such as Tai Po Waterfront Park, Tai Hang Tun, Tap Mun and Shek O Beach, subject to Civil Aviation Department height rules.
kite-flying.venue: Tai Po Waterfront Park / Shek O Beach

fishing-pond.how: Kau Sai Wan Recreational Fishing Wonderland is a stocked fish-farm site near Sai Kung offering a full-day package with boat transfer and gear.
fishing-pond.venue: Kau Sai Wan Recreational Fishing Wonderland

sup-yoga.how: AQUALAND in Sai Kung runs SUP yoga sessions with professional coaches, and Holimood also lists SUP yoga.

surf-simulator.how: Groundswell at AIRSIDE in Kai Tak has a FlowRider standing-wave machine and a beginner surf school.

aerial-silks-circus.how: Aeria Studio (Kennedy Town and Sheung Wan) and Pegasus Studio in Wan Chai teach aerial silks, hoop, trapeze and acrobatics to adults with no experience needed.

bagpipes.how: Pipe Band Hong Kong, formed in 1982, is the largest civilian pipe and drum band in the city, and the Hong Kong Police Pipe Band is a full-time professional band.

chinese-orchestra.how: Community Chinese orchestras exist, but many such as the Police Chinese Culture Club orchestra restrict membership, and the Music Office's Hong Kong Youth Chinese Orchestra takes only people under 25.

choir.how: Hong Kong City Choir is a non-professional choir founded in 1999 with over 80 members.

erhu.how: Fine Music centres in Yuen Long, Sha Tin, Fanling and Tuen Mun offer one-to-one beginner erhu lessons.

guitar.how: Aspire Music in Wan Chai and Parsons Music Academy (about 20 branches) teach guitar to adults and children.

harp.how: HeartStrings Centre teaches harp and lyre from preschool to adult pop-harp courses.

irish-dance.how: O'Connor-Barton Irish Dance holds year-round classes at several Hong Kong locations for ages 3 and up.

piano.how: Parsons Music Academy, Aspire Music and Fine Music all teach piano to beginners, adults and children.

swing-lindy-hop.how: Grappa's Cellar in Central hosts a weekly swing night with a beginners' class before social dancing, and the annual Hong Kong Swing Festival offers workshops.

taiko.how: GEKKO, a taiko ensemble founded in Hong Kong in 2006, performs and competes, including at Japan's Katsugi Oke Battle in 2019.

tap-dance.how: The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts has offered public tap classes since 1994, and Island Dance teaches ISTD tap at many venues.
tap-dance.venue: Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts

batik-painting.how: Batik workshops run occasionally at PMQ, Asia Society Hong Kong and other venues rather than as regular classes.

chinese-calligraphy.how: Art Connect and Communication in Kwun Tong runs English-language brush calligraphy and ink painting classes, and the Hong Kong Palace Museum has held adult masterclasses.

chinese-ink-painting.how: KA Atelier in Wan Chai teaches Chinese painting to adults, and Art Connect in Kwun Tong offers ink painting classes in English.

film-photography-darkroom.how: HKAS runs a one-day black-and-white film developing and enlarger printing workshop, and Camera Film Photo in Cheung Sha Wan hosts darkroom printing workshops.

filmmaking.how: Astro Heart Film Academy and VTC offer part-time film production and compositing courses for adults.

animation-2d.how: Short courses in 2D animation are offered for adults, such as the HKMU/HKAGE programme and CityU's 2D Animation I.

embroidery.how: Make and Do Hong Kong in Chai Wan and Senseless Art Studio in Prince Edward run beginner hand-embroidery workshops.

lampworking.how: The Hong Kong Design Institute (VTC) runs a one-day Level 1 glass lampworking workshop, and Some Thingsss teaches lampworking.

charcoal-life-drawing.how: Weekly open life-drawing sessions run on Tuesday evenings at senselessart Studio in Mong Kok, with short poses suited to beginners.

macrame.how: Make and Do Hong Kong ran a beginner macrame plant-hanger class in Chai Wan, and PMQ has included macrame in its workshop series.

oil-painting.how: Studio 83 teaches classical oil and acrylic painting and Hong Kong Art Tutoring in North Point offers adult courses.

origami.how: Origami is taught in occasional workshops, such as Asia Society Hong Kong's family sessions with a Japanese instructor.

perfumery.how: Hong Kong studios run perfume-blending workshops where participants compose a custom fragrance in about 90 minutes.

rug-tufting.how: Tufting studios such as Tufting Dept run short workshops where beginners tuft a small rug or coaster with a tufting gun.

urban-sketching.how: Urban Sketchers Hong Kong and related groups (Drawn Here, Sketch Hong Kong) hold on-location sketching sessions and introductory workshops.
urban-sketching.venue: Urban Sketchers Hong Kong / HKU SPACE

watercolour-painting.how: The Hong Kong Arts Centre offers multi-week evening courses in botanical watercolour and drawing for adults.
watercolour-painting.venue: Hong Kong Arts Centre / Hong Kong Art School

clay-sculpture.how: Hong Kong Art School and Hong Kong Arts Centre run ceramics and clay workshops, including pottery-throwing courses.

cnc-machining.how: MakerBay is a large Tsuen Wan makerspace with digital fabrication tools and public classes.

robotics-arduino.how: MakerBay and other maker-education groups run Arduino and Raspberry Pi robotics classes open to the public.

cosplay.how: Cosplay centres on large annual conventions such as Ani-Com & Games and Hong Kong Comic Con at the convention centre.

wargaming-warhammer.how: A Games Workshop store in Mong Kok stocks Warhammer ranges and has held painting and modelling workshops.

artisan-bread-baking.how: Cooking studios such as Foodcraft in Kennedy Town and restaurant Roganic run bread and baking classes.

chocolate-making.how: Conspiracy Chocolate in Wong Chuk Hang has run bean-to-bar workshops covering stone-grinding, tempering and moulding.

fermentation-kombucha.how: Lantau Mama, Loula Natural and Roganic offer classes on kombucha, kefir and other ferments.

sourdough-baking.how: MONO runs small-group sourdough masterclasses, and Foodcraft offers a Level 1 sourdough class.

comic-collecting.how: Sino Centre in Mong Kok gathers shops selling comics, anime goods and collectible toys.

vinyl-records.how: Record shops in Sham Shui Po, Yau Ma Tei and Central sell second-hand vinyl across cantopop, jazz and classical.
vinyl-records.venue: Kubrick (Yau Ma Tei) and Sham Shui Po record shops

whale-watching.how: Boat eco-tours from Tung Chung and Tai O watch wild Chinese white dolphins in north Lantau waters (dolphins, not whales).

language-exchange.how: Coffee Break Language Exchange holds weekly meetups where people practise languages in small groups.

philosophy-cafe.how: Hong Kong Philosophy Cafe runs English-language discussion evenings at the Fringe Club.
philosophy-cafe.venue: Hong Kong Philosophy Cafe at Fringe Club

coastal-cleanup.how: A Plastic Ocean Foundation and Beyond Plastic organise regular volunteer clean-ups of non-gazetted beaches with gloves and pickers provided.

running-club.how: CITY RUNNERS (RunOurCity Foundation) runs about 30 neighbourhood running groups with free beginner trial sessions.

tai-chi.how: Asia Society Hong Kong Center has run beginner-friendly tai chi sessions, and free morning tai chi has been held at Hong Kong Park.

canyoning.how: Hong Kong Rock Climbing Adventure leads guided canyoning trips down Ping Nam stream with waterfall abseils.

cable-wakeboarding.how: Wakeboarding is available behind boats at Tai Tam and Tai Po, but no cable park was found.

base-jumping.how: BASE jumping is not offered in Hong Kong because of dense urban airspace and the lack of legal jump sites; it is practised in mainland China and elsewhere.

outdoor-skydiving.how: No skydiving drop zone operates in Hong Kong because of its congested, restricted airspace; tandem jumps are available in mainland China and Southeast Asia.

cave-diving.how: Hong Kong has no flooded cave systems for cave diving; the nearest are in mainland China and elsewhere in Asia.

cave-exploring.how: Hong Kong has no significant cave systems for caving; the nearest are in Guangxi and Guizhou, mainland China.

luge.how: Hong Kong has no luge track or mountain luge facility because it lacks the terrain; the sport is practised in Europe, North America and East Asia.

white-water-rafting.how: Hong Kong has no rivers large enough for white water rafting; the nearest rafting is on rivers in Guangdong, mainland China.

stained-glass.how: Listed in OpenStreetMap: Gold Glass (nearest of 1 tagged venues within 30 km); not checked for current opening.

archery.how: Kyudo (Japanese archery) dojos such as Meiji Jingu Shiseikan and ward sports centres take beginners; Western-style target archery is not documented here.

australian-rules-football.how: Tokyo Goannas (est. 1991) play in the Japan A-League with Japanese and international members, training at Futakotamagawa.

big-wall-climbing.how: No big walls in the Tokyo plain; real big-wall climbing means the Japanese Alps or abroad.

bobsled.how: Needs a purpose-built ice track; none in the Tokyo area (Japan's only track was in Nagano, several hours away).

bouldering.how: B-PUMP Tokyo Akihabara is a large bouldering-only gym with beginner routes, a no-reservation trial and shoe rental.

buzkashi.how: Central Asian horseback game needing a steppe horse culture; not played in Japan.

camel-racing.how: No camel racing in Japan; found in the Gulf states, Australia and Mongolia.

capoeira.how: Samurai Capoeira, founded in Japan, teaches adults and children in Jiyugaoka.

cheese-rolling.how: A single English hill event (Cooper's Hill); no Tokyo equivalent.

curling.how: Tokyo Tatsumi Ice Arena (year-round, opened 2025) supports curling and runs introductory curling trial sessions.

disc-golf.how: UDisc lists several Tokyo-region disc golf courses, including a 9-hole course in Tatsumi-no-mori Seaside Park.
disc-golf.venue: Tatsumi-no-mori Seaside Park disc golf course

elephant-polo.how: Needs working elephants; none are kept for sport in Japan. Played in Nepal, Thailand and India.

horse-riding.how: Horse Club Ginza offers indoor riding-simulator lessons (walk, trot, canter); real riding is at stables outside the city centre.

ice-hockey.how: Tokyo Tatsumi Ice Arena has a main rink and sub-rink supporting ice hockey alongside figure skating and curling.

ice-skating.how: Tokyo Tatsumi Ice Arena offers public skating, an ice skating school with one-coin trial sessions and adults-only night skates.

judo.how: The Kodokan, judo's birthplace, runs a beginner judo school and has at least one English-speaking instructor.

pickleball.how: Hilton Tokyo opened outdoor pickleball courts, and other courts in wards such as Koto and Minato are listed.

rugby.how: International clubs such as Tokyo Gaijin RFC play in amateur leagues and welcome foreigners; most clubs train on Sundays at rented pitches.

skateboarding.how: Miyashita Park's rooftop skatepark has a bowl and stair sets, with a small admission fee and free helmet loan.

ski-jumping.how: Needs a jump hill with snow; none near Tokyo (nearest are in Nagano and Hokkaido).

snowboarding.how: No natural snow in Tokyo; the nearest snowboarding resorts (e.g. Yuzawa in Niigata) are about 90 minutes away by Shinkansen.

taekwondo.how: A beginner-friendly taekwondo class run via a Tokyo international meetup group meets in Akihabara.

ultimate-frisbee.how: Tokyo Ultimate holds bi-weekly pickup sessions open to all, plus league play.

fishing.how: Saltwater fishing from the Nishi Nagisa artificial tidal flat at Kasai Rinkai Park; Wakasu Seaside Park rents rods at the breakwater.

mangrove-sea-kayaking.how: No mangroves in the Tokyo area; Japan's mangroves are on Okinawa and the Amami islands.

hang-gliding.how: Needs launch slopes; the nearest sites (e.g. Mt Tsukuba) are roughly 1.5 to 2 hours from Tokyo.

kayaking.how: Guided kayak tours on Tokyo's canals and the Sumida River, with a beginner route past Nihonbashi Bridge and Skytree.

fishing-pond.how: Tsuribori Musashinoen in Suginami is a paid fishing pond beside the Zenpukuji river; 2016 source, so status should be rechecked.

pedal-boating.how: Inokashira Park's pond has swan pedal boats, standard pedal boats and rowboats rented by the half hour.

rowing.how: Toda Rowing Course in Saitama (Olympic venue) hosts rowing clubs; Tokyo's Sea Forest Waterway ran a 2022 beginner commemorative regatta but regular public rowing is limited.

scuba-diving.how: PADI shops such as EastDive run Discover Scuba and Open Water courses with indoor pool sessions in Tokyo; open-water dives happen on the Izu Peninsula.

stand-up-paddleboarding.how: ZAC runs a one-hour beginner Tokyo SUP Experience on the Kyu-Naka River.

surfing-ocean.how: Tokyo Bay is sheltered with no ocean swell; the nearest surf breaks are in Shonan (Kanagawa) and Chiba, roughly 1 to 1.5 hours away.

windsurfing.how: The 85 Club windsurfing school gives beginner lessons at Kemigawa Beach on Tokyo Bay in Chiba, about 30 km away.

bullfighting.how: No bullfighting in Japan; found in Spain, Portugal and Latin America.

canyoning.how: Needs gorges; Canyons Okutama runs tours in west Tokyo about 90 minutes from the centre.

cave-diving.how: No flooded cave systems near Tokyo; the nearest cave diving is in Okinawa and Shikoku.

cave-exploring.how: Limestone caves such as Nippara Cave are in the Okutama mountains, around 2 hours from central Tokyo.

dog-sledding.how: Needs snow and sled-dog culture; nearest is Hokkaido.

glacier-trekking.how: Japan has no accessible glaciers for trekking; nearest alternatives are in the Alps or New Zealand.

indoor-skydiving.how: FlyStation Japan in Koshigaya, Saitama has a 20 m transparent wind tunnel with first-flight and flight-school plans (2019 source).

luge.how: Needs a purpose-built track; none in the Tokyo area.

mountaineering.how: Alpine mountaineering means the Japanese Alps, around 3 hours away; Okutama peaks are hiking terrain.

outdoor-skydiving.how: Tokyo Skydiving Club at Honda Airport in Saitama offers tandem jumps and AFF, about 40 km north of Tokyo (beyond the metro radius).

paragliding.how: Needs launch slopes; the nearest schools are around Mt Tsukuba and the Fuji foothills, 1.5 to 2 hours away.

rodeo.how: No rodeo tradition in Japan; found in North America, Australia and parts of Latin America.

safari.how: No free-roaming wildlife to see; nearest equivalent is drive-through safari parks, about 2 hours away.

sandboarding-desert.how: No dunes near Tokyo; the Tottori Sand Dunes are far to the west.

snow-skiing.how: No natural snow in Tokyo; the nearest ski resorts (e.g. Gala Yuzawa) are about 90 minutes away by Shinkansen.

volcano-boarding.how: Volcano boarding is done on Cerro Negro in Nicaragua; no equivalent in Japan.

white-water-rafting.how: Rafting needs rapids; the Tama River in Okutama (about 1.5 hours away) and Tone River in Gunma are the nearest.

hiking.how: Mount Takao in Hachioji has eight marked trails and is about an hour from central Tokyo by train.

trail-running.how: Mount Takao's eight mountain trails, reached in about an hour from central Tokyo, are used for hiking and trail running.

toy-collecting.how: Nakano Broadway's upper floors are packed with shops selling figurines, anime merchandise and collectibles, including Mandarake annexes dedicated to toy robots and action figures.

comic-collecting.how: Mandarake's Nakano Broadway store and its specialist annexes sell used manga, comics and doujinshi.

rug-tufting.how: Tufting studio KEKE ran first-time workshops where visitors tuft a small rug from their own design (online booking); the listing is from 2021.

pottery-wheel.how: Atelier Little Pottery Studio in Kichijoji teaches wheel throwing to enthusiasts and novices; several other Minato-ku schools offer one-day trial courses.

pottery-handbuilding.how: Atelier Little Pottery Studio in Kichijoji teaches hand-building alongside wheel throwing under experienced instructors.

stand-up-comedy.how: Tokyo Comedy Bar runs two English-language open mic nights a week plus showcases, so beginners can try a set.

improv-comedy.how: Tokyo Comedy Bar hosts regular improv shows and occasional improv classes and workshops.

salsa-bachata.how: Studio JBA runs salsa or bachata lessons on most nights, usually a 7pm beginner class followed by social dancing.

taiko.how: Studio Hougaku Academy teaches taiko from beginner to advanced with bookable one-time trial lessons; sticks are included.

tap-dance.how: Ance Space Yoyogi is a rental studio used for lessons from tap to house dance and capoeira.

swing-lindy-hop.how: Tokyo Swing Dance Society ran Swing Sundays and Swing Night lessons in English and Japanese (2014 listing).

ballet.how: Architanz offers drop-in ballet classes, with most teachers speaking English (2014 listing).

flamenco.how: Fitness Club Hiroo lists flamenco among its dance classes (2014 listing).

bookbinding.how: Ito Bindery, a family-run bindery in Sumida, hosts a beginner notebook-making experience in Japanese and English.

chinese-ink-painting.how: Art Party Tokyo has run beginner calligraphy and sumi-e workshops held in English with no experience needed (2025 sessions listed).

chinese-calligraphy.how: Only Japanese calligraphy (shodo) was found, taught in an English-language beginner workshop at Art Party Tokyo rather than a Chinese-calligraphy school.

leatherwork.how: Hiro Workshop in Kichijoji teaches small leather goods at all skill levels, with drop-in during opening hours.

jewellery-silversmithing.how: Hiro Workshop in Kichijoji also teaches brass and silver jewellery making at all skill levels.

film-photography-darkroom.how: Paper Pool in Yutenji rents a monochrome darkroom by the half hour with chemicals supplied; Tokyo has other rental darkrooms.

weaving.how: Saori Tokyo runs two-hour Saori weaving classes Tuesday to Saturday, with staff demonstrating each step and only a little English spoken.

origami.how: Ochanomizu Origami Kaikan runs monthly origami workshops that can be taken in English or Japanese.

animation-2d.how: Tokyo Animation College offers 2- and 3-year full-time animation courses; no short hobby course was confirmed.

photography.how: Japanorama gives English-language photography lessons and photowalks for beginners (rates from a 2016 page).

urban-sketching.how: FabCafe Tokyo hosts a free monthly drop-in drawing meetup (drink required, booking needed); the listing seen is from 2023.

blacksmithing.how: Hirata Bladesmiths in Ome offers a roughly two-hour knife-forging experience for visitors rather than ongoing smithing classes.

freshwater-fishing.how: Benkei Fishing Club, a pond in central Tokyo, charges by the half hour and rents rods; bait fishing is beginner-friendly.

stargazing.how: Roppongi Tenmon Club holds monthly and moon-viewing sessions on the Tokyo City View deck, limited by city light pollution.

geocaching.how: Tokyo has many active geocaches, including one by the Hachiko statue in Shibuya and the most-favourited cache in Japan at Kaminarimon, Asakusa.

nature-guided-walks.how: English-speaking guides lead hiking tours of Mount Takao from Shinjuku Station.

birdwatching.how: Tokyo Port Wild Bird Park, a Wild Bird Society of Japan sanctuary on reclaimed bay land, is open daily except Mondays for a small entry fee.

butterfly-watching.how: The free 599 Museum at the foot of Mount Takao has a large insect section with butterflies displayed by species.

sneaker-collecting.how: Harajuku and Shibuya have dozens of sneaker shops such as Kicks Lab, Worm and Kith Tokyo (browsing is free; purchases cost extra).

watch-collecting.how: Nakano Broadway hosts several vintage and second-hand watch shops such as Jack Road, alongside shops in Ginza, Morishita and Shinjuku.

trading-cards.how: Akihabara has many card shops; Card Lab (C-Labo) in the Radio Kaikan building has a 64-seat dueling venue.
